title: Cut a scene to read it closely
statement: Have learners cut a scene to half its length and defend the most important line they kept and the most useless one they cut: deciding what stays forces close reading.
example: In one guide, groups cut a scene of roughly 200 lines to around 100.
detail: A published classroom guide from the Folger Shakespeare Library, kept in the Grade 9 sources, holds that students asked to cut lines from any text must read closely to decide what stays and what goes (`g9/sources/Cutting-a-Scene-Othello-1.1.pdf`, pdftotext lines 3-4). Its groups read a scene aloud and cut it in half, from roughly 200 lines to around 100, keeping what they judge most important, and each student then writes a reflection defending the most important line saved and the most useless line cut (lines 45-54, 69-75 and 104-109). It is a practice guide, not a study, and gives no web address or DOI of its own.
against: The guide reports no measured effect.

evidence.quote: When students are asked to cut (omit, scratch out) lines from any text, they must do all kinds of close reading in order to make their decisions about what stays and what goes.
Explain that their job is to cut the scene in half: to shorten the scene without losing what is most important in the scene.
This complex scene, which opens the play Othello, is roughly 200 lines. Students’ cut scenes should be around 100 lines.
What is the most important line they saved? What makes this line so important to your scene? What is the most useless line they cut? Why was it useless in this scene?
Get students defending specific choices in this informal reflection
